questions.sub_skill: Implement conditional access for Microsoft Entra Agent ID
questions.prompt: Your tenant's only Conditional Access policy requires MFA for All users. You deploy an autonomous agent that acquires tokens with its own agent identity. Which statement is correct?
options: The agent is blocked because it cannot complete the MFA challenge; exclude agents from the policy
The policy does not apply: agent identities are not users, so the agent gets tokens with no Conditional Access until you create policies that target agent identities
The policy applies, and the agent satisfies MFA with its blueprint's credential
Conditional Access cannot be applied to agents in any form
questions.explanation: An autonomous agent's token subject is its agent identity. Policies assigned to All users do not include agent identities - and Microsoft notes they do not include agents' user accounts either. Agents cannot answer MFA anyway. The fix is agent policies: block all agent identities except approved ones (selected individually, by blueprint or by custom security attribute), and block high-risk agents.
why_not: All users policies do not target agent identities, so the MFA policy never evaluates the agent's token request - nothing blocks it, and nothing protects it.
A blueprint's credential proves the agent's identity; it is not a second factor - and the user policy does not target agents in the first place.
Conditional Access for agents exists: policies can target agent identities, blueprints, or agents' user accounts, with the right licensing.
questions.scenario_clue: An autonomous agent using its own agent identity - the token subject is not a user, so a policy scoped to All users never reaches it.

questions.sub_skill: Analyze blast radius for security risks related to Entra Agent ID by using Defender XDR
questions.prompt: Two agents have identical tools and grounding sources. One runs on-behalf-of a signed-in user; the other is autonomous. How do their blast radii compare?
options: Identical, because the tools are identical
The autonomous agent's is larger in every case
The on-behalf-of agent's varies with whoever is talking to it, because it acts with that user's permissions; the autonomous agent's is fixed at whatever its own identity holds
Neither has a blast radius until a credential is compromised
questions.explanation: An on-behalf-of agent acts with the signed-in user's identity and permissions, so its reach changes per user. An autonomous agent has no user context, so its own assignments are the whole of its reach. Blast radius here is about subversion of instructions, not credential theft.
why_not: Identical tools do not mean identical reach. The on-behalf-of agent acts with each user's permissions, so its reach changes per user.
Not in every case. An on-behalf-of agent serving a highly privileged user can reach more than an autonomous agent with narrow assignments.
Blast radius here is about subverting the agent's instructions, not stealing a credential. It exists as soon as the agent can act.
questions.scenario_clue: "on-behalf-of a signed-in user" versus "autonomous" - delegated access follows the user, so the blast radius changes with who is signed in.
questions.misconception: Identical tools mean identical blast radius

questions.sub_skill: Enable and configure real-time protection for Microsoft Copilot Studio agents
questions.prompt: You turn on Copilot Studio real-time protection in the Microsoft Defender portal. Agents in your existing environment are protected, but agents in a newly created Power Platform environment are not. What is missing, and what tells you protection is live?
options: A Copilot Studio licence for the new environment; the agent would show as Unlicensed
The Power Platform administrator's threat detection setup for that environment - it is configured per environment; the Copilot Studio step in Defender shows Connected once onboarding is complete
An Entra Agent ID blueprint for each agent; the agent would not appear in the registry
A Defender for Cloud Apps file policy; the agent would show as Discovered
questions.explanation: Real-time protection is two-sided: the Defender portal step and the Power Platform admin center step (Security > Threat detection > Additional threat detection). The Power Platform side is configured per environment, with no tenant-wide switch, so a new environment needs it too. Connected status on the Copilot Studio step confirms onboarding.
why_not: Licensing is not the missing piece. The new environment has not been connected to the threat detection provider.
Agent identities and blueprints are not what enables runtime protection for Copilot Studio agents.
A Defender for Cloud Apps policy is not what is missing; the per-environment Power Platform step is.
questions.scenario_clue: Protection works in one environment but not a new one - the hint that the setting is per environment.

questions.prompt: An agent created eight months ago by a departed employee still runs nightly with nobody accountable. Which mechanisms should have prevented this?
options: A Conditional Access policy blocking high-risk agent identities
An entitlement management access package with an expiry, plus a sponsorship lifecycle workflow that transfers sponsorship when a sponsor leaves
Advanced real-time protection on the agent's runtime
Assigning the agent to a dedicated Security Copilot workspace
questions.explanation: Access packages make an agent's access expire unless someone re-confirms it, and lifecycle workflow templates for sponsorship transfer exist specifically to prevent orphaned agents. Conditional Access governs how an agent gets tokens, not who is accountable for it.
why_not: Conditional Access governs how an agent gets tokens, not who is accountable for it.
Runtime protection inspects what an agent does while it runs. It does not expire access or transfer ownership.
A Security Copilot workspace has nothing to do with an agent's ownership or access expiry.
questions.scenario_clue: "departed employee" and "nobody accountable" - that is a lifecycle failure: access that never expires and a sponsor who was never replaced.
questions.misconception: Runtime protection or Conditional Access fixes ownership problems

questions.sub_skill: Manage agents in Microsoft 365 admin center
questions.prompt: Any licensed user in your tenant can build a Copilot Studio agent. Where do you take a tenant-wide inventory and block ones you do not want?
options: Entra admin center, under Agent ID blueprints
Microsoft 365 admin center agent management
Defender portal, under Security for AI agents
Power Platform admin center environments only
questions.explanation: The Microsoft 365 admin center provides the tenant-wide agent inventory with ownership, risk indicators, and the ability to block or disable. Shadow agents are the governance problem here, and you cannot govern an inventory you have not taken.
why_not: Agent ID blueprints are identity constructs in Entra. The tenant-wide agent inventory with block and disable is in the Microsoft 365 admin center.
The Defender portal is where runtime protection is configured, not where the tenant-wide inventory with block and disable lives.
Power Platform environments are only part of the picture. The tenant-wide inventory is in the Microsoft 365 admin center.
questions.scenario_clue: "tenant-wide inventory" of agents "any licensed user" can build, and "block" - that is agent management in the Microsoft 365 admin center.
questions.misconception: Power Platform environments are the only place to govern Copilot Studio agents
